Our releases happen in two steps: first we upload every new asset under a versioned name, then we switch the manifest to point at those new names. We never overwrite or immediately delete the old assets.

The upload comes first because the manifest switch is what makes a release live. Once a browser fetches the new manifest, it immediately requests the files it names. If those files weren't already uploaded, the browser would get missing assets and a broken page. Uploading everything first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when the switch happens. Versioned names also mean the upload can't disturb anything currently in use, so we can do it before the release goes live.

We keep the old assets because some browsers will have fetched the previous manifest before the switch. Those browsers will keep requesting the old names. If we removed the old files, those users would hit missing assets in the middle of a session. Leaving them available means both the old and new manifests resolve fully, so nobody breaks during the changeover.

The upload comes first because the manifest is what tells browsers which files to load. If we switched it before the new files existed, a browser could fetch the new manifest, request files that aren't there yet, and get broken pages. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when it goes live. Versioned names let the new files sit alongside the current ones without overwriting anything that's being served.

We keep the old assets because some browsers already fetched the previous manifest before the switch. Those browsers will keep requesting the old names. If we deleted those files, those users would get missing assets until they reloaded and picked up the new manifest. Keeping the old files lets both manifests work during the transition.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first so the manifest never references a file that isn't there yet. If we switched first, a browser could fetch the new manifest, request a new asset that hasn't finished uploading, and get a 404 or a broken page. With versioned names, uploading is harmless on its own: nothing points at the new files until the manifest switches, and at that moment they're all already in place.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the previous one. Those browsers will keep requesting the old versioned names, for example when lazy-loading a script or opening another page. If we deleted the old files, those requests would fail mid-session. Keeping them lets every browser finish using a consistent set of assets, whichever manifest it fetched.

Every release ships its assets under new versioned filenames (for example, `app.3f9c2.js` instead of overwriting `app.js`), so new files never collide with ones already being served. Once every new asset is uploaded, we update the manifest to point at the new names. The manifest switch is the moment the release goes live.

The upload has to come first because the manifest is what browsers follow. If we switched it before the files existed, any browser that loaded the new manifest would request assets that aren't there yet and get 404s, leaving the page broken until the upload finished. Uploading first means every name the new manifest references is already available when the manifest goes live.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that are already running. A browser that loaded the page before the switch still holds the previous manifest and will keep requesting the old filenames, for example when it lazy-loads a chunk or navigates within the app. If we deleted those files at release time, those sessions would break mid-use. Leaving them in place lets old and new clients coexist safely.
